notes: Landmark Yarl's Wood riot appeal; witness coaching and juror misconduct guidance from Judge LJ.

enrichment.short_title: Momodou: Yarl's Wood riot convictions upheld despite witness coaching
key_facts: Henry Momodou and Beher Limani were convicted of violent disorder after a four-month trial arising from the February 2002 riot at Yarl's Wood Immigration Detention Centre.
Group 4 arranged Bond Solon witness training for prosecution staff using an inappropriate case study; sixteen potential witnesses received training before the programme was stopped.
Twenty-two DCOs also received cognitive therapy from Dr McGurk after the disturbance, raising contamination concerns.
Jurors complained about fellow jurors' conduct during the lengthy trial; the judge investigated without discharging the jury.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal with leave against conviction and four-year sentences for violent disorder after conviction at Harrow Crown Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals against conviction and sentence dismissed; convictions and four-year sentences upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Witness training or coaching for criminal witnesses is not permitted and is distinct from lawful witness familiarisation; pre-trial therapy must be disclosed so its impact can be assessed at trial; a judge may properly investigate juror complaints without discharging the jury where fairness is preserved.
legal_issues: Whether Bond Solon witness training rendered convictions unsafe
Whether McGurk cognitive therapy contaminated prosecution evidence
Whether removal of detainee witnesses amounted to abuse of process
Whether juror misconduct communications required discharge of the jury
Whether four-year sentences were manifestly excessive or disparate
linked_authorities: Richardson [1971] CAR 244
Shaw [2002] EWCA Crim 3004
Skinner [1994] 99 CAR 212

confidence.notes: Detailed appellate reasoning on coaching, therapy and juror issues with clear dismissal of appeals.

notes: GMC interim suspension extension after manslaughter conviction; Stanley Burnton J's proportionality analysis.

enrichment.short_title: GMC v Walker: nine-month extension of interim suspension after manslaughter
key_facts: Dr Walker remained interim suspended after a 2003 GMC Interim Orders Committee order following criminal proceedings.
He pleaded guilty to one count of manslaughter relating to a patient death and received a 21-month suspended sentence in June 2004.
The conviction triggered mandatory referral to the Fitness to Practise Panel; additional CV allegations remained under GMC examination.
The Interim Orders Committee directed the Registrar to seek a High Court extension because the interim order expired on 8 January 2005.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court application under section 41A(6) of the Medical Act 1983 to extend interim suspension pending Fitness to Practise proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Interim suspension extended for nine months; Interim Orders Committee invited to review within two months; no order as to costs.
enrichment.ratio: Considerable weight attaches to Interim Orders Committee decisions not challenged as unlawful; where a doctor has been convicted of manslaughter and sentenced to imprisonment, even if suspended, extension of interim suspension may be a proportionate response pending Fitness to Practise proceedings.
legal_issues: Whether interim suspension should be extended pending Fitness to Practise Panel hearing
Whether the GMC sought an excessive twelve-month extension
Whether the doctor could practise non-surgical medicine while suspended
Whether costs should follow the event

confidence.notes: Clear facts, statutory basis and remedial order; some procedural background remains complex.

notes: Attorney General unduly lenient reference; sustained sexual abuse of granddaughter.

enrichment.short_title: AG Ref 125/2004: unduly lenient sentence for grandfather's sexual abuse

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Court Services Act 2000

key_facts: A 70-year-old grandfather was convicted of indecent assault, indecency with a child and attempted rape against his granddaughter aged six-and-a-half to thirteen.
Abuse occurred hundreds of times at his home over eight years, escalating from touching to digital penetration and attempted penile penetration.
Judge Neligan sentenced him to three years' imprisonment on the attempted rape counts with ancillary Sexual Offences Prevention and disqualification orders.
The offender denied misconduct, claimed impotence since 1987, and showed no remorse; his wife suffered serious ill-health.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 alleging unduly lenient sentences at Maidstone Crown Court.
enrichment.outcome: Reference allowed; three-year sentence on attempted rape counts quashed and substituted with four-and-a-half years' imprisonment concurrent, with double jeopardy taken into account.
enrichment.ratio: A total sentence of three years failed adequately to reflect the gravity of sustained familial sexual abuse of a child; an expected sentence of about six years before double jeopardy justified substitution of four-and-a-half years on the attempted rape counts.
legal_issues: Whether the three-year total sentence was unduly lenient
Application of Millberry starting points for child sexual offences
Weight of aggravating features including breach of trust and escalating conduct
Whether double jeopardy should prevent intervention
linked_authorities: R v Millberry [2003] 1 Cr App R 396
Attorney-General's Reference No 52 of 2003 (R v Webb) [2003] EWCA Crim 3731
Attorney-General's Reference No 31 and Ors of 2004 [2004] EWCA Crim 1934

confidence.notes: Facts, sentencing analysis and substituted term are clearly stated.

notes: Leading Sexual Offences Act 2003 sentencing guidance; four consolidated appeals.

enrichment.short_title: Corran and others: sentencing guidance under Sexual Offences Act 2003

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Court Services Act 2000

key_facts: Four unrelated sentencing appeals were heard together concerning offences under the Sexual Offences Act 2003 in force from 1 May 2004.
Corran, aged twenty, had consensual sex with a twelve-year-old girl who claimed to be sixteen; he received two years' detention for section 5 rape.
Cutler, aged thirty-five, had repeated penetrative sexual activity with a thirteen-year-old girl in a position of trust.
Heard received extended sentences for sexual activity with a fourteen-year-old and indecent images; Williams received life imprisonment for abusing an eleven-year-old boy.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Consolidated Court of Appeal sentencing appeals and applications for leave concerning new Sexual Offences Act 2003 offences.
enrichment.outcome: Corran's sentence reduced to a six-month conditional discharge; Cutler's leave refused; Heard's extended sentence reduced to six years total; Williams' life sentence upheld but notional determinate term reduced from nine to six years.
enrichment.ratio: Section 5 rape of a child under thirteen attracts a wide sentencing bracket with custody usually required; consent and relative age are material mitigating factors for young defendants; Parliament's increased maximum penalties for sections 9 and 10 must be reflected; Millberry aggravating and mitigating features remain applicable.
legal_issues: Sentencing for section 5 rape of a child under thirteen where victim consented and appeared older
Whether increased maximum sentences for sections 9 and 10 require higher terms than pre-Act offences
Appropriate extended sentences for repeat sexual offending against children
Whether digital anal penetration justified a discretionary life sentence
Construction of notional determinate terms where life imprisonment is imposed
linked_authorities: Attorney-General's Reference No 104 of 2004 (R v Garvey) [2004] EWCA Crim 2672
R v Millberry [2003] 2 Cr App R(S) 142
R v Wheaton [2004] EWCA Crim 2270

confidence.notes: Comprehensive guidance across four cases though individual outcomes vary.

notes: Out-of-time VAT judicial review renewal; Moses J refuses permission.

enrichment.short_title: Tebbut: judicial review refused over lost VAT payments to Customs
key_facts: Two former traders claimed they paid two £5,000 cheques in 1991 towards VAT liability that Customs and Excise failed to credit.
A VAT Tribunal in 1994-1996 determined undeclared tax liability of about £4,316 plus interest after partial assessment quashing.
County court private law claims were struck out in 1998 for no cause of action; a judge suggested negotiation with Customs.
Customs made a without-prejudice settlement offer in 1999 to call matters quits; the claimants did not accept and sought Ombudsman and judicial review relief.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to judicial review following refusal by Bennett J on the papers.
enrichment.outcome: Permission refused; complaints out of time and no basis for judicial review over Customs' conduct or failure to settle.
enrichment.ratio: Where alleged maladministration by Customs occurred many years ago and no recent decision is susceptible to review, judicial review is unavailable; a disputed historical tax payment and failed private law claim cannot be revived through this court as a last resort.
legal_issues: Whether Customs' failure to credit VAT payments was maladministration
Whether the claim was out of time for judicial review
Whether the court had jurisdiction over a course of conduct rather than a identifiable decision
Whether Customs' without-prejudice settlement offer affected the claim

confidence.notes: Clear refusal on time and merits though underlying payment dispute remains factually contested.

notes: Care proceedings appeal; section 34(4) contact termination refused.

enrichment.short_title: Re H: refusal of section 34(4) order terminating parental contact
key_facts: Two children aged five and three were committed to care with an adoption plan after a long family history including a prior care order on the elder child.
The local authority sought a section 34(4) order to suspend parental contact during transition from foster care to adoptive placement, not permanent termination.
Expert evidence supported continuing post-adoption contact with the parents, who were not predictably disruptive of placement.
No adopters had been identified and the judge considered adoption uncertain; he refused the powerful section 34(4) order.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Local authority appeal against refusal of an application under section 34(4) of the Children Act 1989 to authorise termination of parental contact.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; county court judge's refusal of the section 34(4) order upheld.
enrichment.ratio: A section 34(4) order authorising termination of contact is appropriate where there is no likelihood of rehabilitation and closed adoption is planned; it should not be granted prematurely for uncertain future use to ease local authority placement logistics where post-adoption contact is envisaged and parents are not disruptive.
legal_issues: Whether a section 34(4) order was needed to secure adoptive placement
Whether the order was premature where no adopters were identified
Whether post-adoption contact plans affected the application
Application of Re L, Re T and Re S principles on section 34(4) orders
linked_authorities: Re S (Care: Parental Contact) [2004] EWCA Civ 1397

confidence.notes: Clear discretionary analysis with established authority applied consistently.

notes: Bullock/Sanderson costs appeal; Peter Gibson LJ dismisses.

enrichment.short_title: Irvine v Met Police: no Bullock order for unsuccessful defendant costs
key_facts: Police constable Michael Irvine tripped on stair carpet at Trinity Road Police Station and retired on medical grounds.
He sued the Metropolitan Police Commissioner, property manager Carillion and flooring contractor Town and Country Flooring.
He succeeded against the Commissioner for breach of statutory duty under workplace regulations but failed in negligence against all defendants.
The judge ordered Irvine to pay the second and third defendants' costs rather than making a Bullock or Sanderson order against the Commissioner.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against refusal to make a Bullock or Sanderson costs order transferring successful defendants' costs to the unsuccessful first defendant.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; claimant ordered to pay second and third defendants' costs; no Bullock or Sanderson order made.
enrichment.ratio: Bullock and Sanderson orders are ordinarily for claims against defendants in the alternative; where a claimant pursues separate and unconnected causes of action against multiple defendants and fails against some, it is not unjust to apply the general rule that the unsuccessful claimant pays successful defendants' costs.
legal_issues: Whether Bullock or Sanderson orders survived the CPR
Whether it was reasonable to join Carillion and Town and Country Flooring
Whether claims were in the alternative or cumulative
Whether the first defendant blaming others made joinder reasonable
Application of CPR 44.3 discretion on costs
linked_authorities: Bullock v London General Omnibus Company [1907] 1 KB 264
Sanderson v Blyth Theatre Company [1903] 2 KB 533
Mulready v JH & W Bell Ltd [1953] 2 All ER 215
Bankamerica Finance Ltd v Nock [1988] AC 1002

notes: Guidance on CPR 52.13 second appeals; asbestos mesothelioma limitation case.

enrichment.short_title: Uphill v BRB: second appeal permission refused on CPR 52.13
key_facts: Malcolm Uphill died of mesothelioma in 1999 after asbestos exposure as a British Transport Commission apprentice from 1951 to 1956.
His widow's claim form was issued on 8 August 2002 but not served within four months; extension to 1 April 2003 was granted without notice.
Claim form was posted to loss adjusters Miller Fisher rather than the defendant or its solicitors; defendant acknowledged service without contesting jurisdiction under CPR 11.
First appeal judge held defendant waived challenge to service; Court of Appeal guidance on CPR 52.13 second appeals was sought.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal on a second appeal against refusal to set aside extension of time and service rulings in asbestos negligence claim.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused on all grounds; guidance given on CPR 52.13(2) meaning of important point of principle and compelling reason.
enrichment.ratio: CPR 52.13(2)(a) requires an unestablished important point of principle or practice, not mere misapplication of established guidance; compelling reason under (2)(b) is exceptional and usually requires very high prospects of success or procedural unfairness; failure to cite Hashtroodi before first appeal judgment sealed may negate compelling reason.
legal_issues: Meaning of important point of principle or practice under CPR 52.13(2)(a)
Scope of compelling reason under CPR 52.13(2)(b)
Whether Hashtroodi required setting aside extension of time for service
Whether defendant waived right to challenge service under CPR 11
Whether service on loss adjusters was valid
linked_authorities: Hashtroodi v Hancock [2004] EWCA Civ 652
Tanfern Limited v Cameron-MacDonald [2000] 1 WLR 1311
Anderton v Clwyd County Council [2002] EWCA Civ 933

confidence.notes: Authoritative CPR 52.13 guidance intended for citation; fact-specific refusal clearly reasoned.

notes: Contract rectification appeal; unilateral mistake claim fails.

enrichment.short_title: Wimpey v VIC: rectification refused for overage payment formula
key_facts: George Wimpey agreed to buy the VIC Industrial Estate in Erith for £2.25 million plus 50% overage if flat sale prices exceeded a base figure of about £20.6 million.
The written contract formula for deferred overage on changed flat sizes omitted enhancement premiums (+E) that had been discussed in negotiations.
Deputy High Court judge ordered rectification based on VIC's unilateral mistake, believing Wimpey shared the intended formula.
Wimpey had paid £45,000 under the rectification order pending appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by VIC against order rectifying the 1999 land sale contract for unilateral mistake as to the overage payment formula.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; rectification order set aside and action dismissed; Wimpey to repay £45,000 plus interest and pay costs.
enrichment.ratio: Rectification for unilateral mistake requires convincing proof that the counterparty knew or ought to have known of the mistake and failed to draw attention to it; absent proof that Wimpey intended terms other than the written formula, rectification cannot substitute negotiated enhancement premiums into the overage clause.
legal_issues: Whether rectification was available for unilateral mistake on overage formula
Whether Wimpey knew VIC intended '+E' enhancements in the deferred payment calculation
Whether Mr Ketteridge's understanding was Wimpey's collective intention
Effect of changes to flat numbers and sizes on overage calculation

confidence.notes: Clear appellate reversal with detailed contractual analysis though negotiation facts are intricate.

notes: Dow Jones internet libel; proceedings stayed for abuse and insignificant publication.

enrichment.short_title: Dow Jones v Jameel: libel proceedings stayed for insignificant publication
key_facts: Yousef Jameel sued Dow Jones over a Wall Street Journal Online article listing alleged al Qaeda financiers including his name on the Golden Chain list.
The article was posted on New Jersey web servers in March 2003 and accessed by about 5,000 UK subscribers before removal from the active site.
Dow Jones did not seek to justify the defamation; it relied on responsible journalism in reporting US government statements.
Eady J struck out parts of the defence and the claimant sought substantial damages; total UK readership was minimal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against interlocutory rulings and application to stay libel proceedings as an abuse of process for insignificant publication within the jurisdiction.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; proceedings stayed as an abuse of process; insignificant publication in England did not justify continuation.
enrichment.ratio: Where defamatory internet publication within the jurisdiction is minimal and there is no real prospect of significant further reputational harm or a useful injunction, permitting libel proceedings to continue amounts to an abuse of process incompatible with the need for proportionality in defamation litigation.
legal_issues: Whether publication within the jurisdiction was real and substantial
Whether proceedings were an abuse of process for insignificant publication
Whether Dow Jones could restrict UK access to online archives
Whether injunction against republication would be practicable or valuable
Appeal against Eady J's interlocutory rulings on the defence
linked_authorities: Mohammed Abdul Latif Jameel v The Wall Street Journal Europe SPRL [2005] EWCA Civ 74

confidence.notes: Clear stay decision with detailed proportionality reasoning on internet libel.
